title: Geometry — Test #2: Vocabulary
subtitle: Sections 1-1 to 1-4 · 15 terms
notes: Source is Study Guide #2 Part I, sections 1-1 to 1-4, two word banks (7 terms + 8 terms).

reference/ holds THREE scans. Two are the same Part I worksheet (the second is Part I after corrections). The third is the real Part II. Part II uses the SAME two word banks and the SAME 15 terms as Part I — only the order of the blanks changes — so this file covers both parts and needs no additions. Part II states 1f as "equal shape and size" where Part I says "same shape and size"; the term is Congruent either way.

IMPORTANT: there is NO teacher answer key for this test — only the student's completed worksheet. These definitions were derived independently from the printed prompts, using the fact that each word bank is a bijection (7 words for 7 blanks, 8 for 8), so each term is used exactly once.

Blanks 1a and 1f were SWAPPED on the first scan: "Collinear" was written for "a finite portion of a line" (that is Segment) and "segment" for "two or more points on the same line" (that is Collinear). The second scan in reference/ ("Part 2") is the same worksheet after corrections, and it corrects exactly these two blanks to Segment and Collinear — confirming what this file already said. Do not "fix" it back to the first scan.
Terms are capitalized as the printed word bank capitalizes them.
confusables notes are shown after a second miss.

Part II independently confirms the Part I corrections: its blank 1c, "a finite portion of a line", is answered Segment, and its 1b, "two or more points on the same line", is answered Collinear — both correct on that worksheet.

confusables.note: The prefix "non-" is the whole difference; collinear points share one line, noncollinear ones do not.
Distinguish by how many endpoints each has: a line none, a ray one, a segment two.
Order them by measure: under 90, exactly 90, between 90 and 180, exactly 180.
All are points; what differs is where. A vertex is where two rays meet; a midpoint is the center of a segment; a point is any location at all.
One is the figure, the other is the ray that cuts that figure in half.
